stops.name: The Val Sans Retour, the curse cast
stops.campa: In the valley beyond the mirror, Morgan raises walls no eye can see: whichever knight enters here having ever been false to his love, in deed or only in thought, finds he cannot find the way out again, and does not himself understand why his feet keep turning him back to where he started. She sets a stone at the entrance that names the place for what it now is, the Val sans Retour, the Valley of No Return, and swears the enchantment will hold until a knight comes through it whose love has never once wavered. She does not expect to meet such a man; she has not yet heard of Lancelot.

stops.name: The Val Sans Retour, the prisoners of the trials
stops.campa: Year on year the valley fills. Two hundred and fifty-three knights wander inside it, held seventeen years, each caught the same way, each free within the trap to eat and dance and speak with the others but never to leave, and Morgan provides for every one of them as a hostess provides for guests who will simply never go home. Even her own son Yvain rides in to try the trial and fails it like the rest; the Duke of Clarence passes the dragons and is beaten at the pool. Dragons guard one approach, a wall of fire another, a cliff-drowned pool a third, and no one yet has passed all three.

stops.name: The Val Sans Retour, Lancelot breaks the spell
stops.campa: Lancelot rides into the valley not knowing what it is, and where every wall of fire and every dragon has turned back every other man, they open for him because in his whole heart, whatever else is broken in it, he has never once wavered from Guinevere. The valley's two hundred and fifty-three knights walk free the same hour, laughing and weeping at a gate that has held them for years. Morgan, watching her enchantment fail on the one man in the world whose fidelity truly cannot be pried loose, does the only thing left to do: she closes a golden ring on his finger, and if she cannot keep the valley, she means to keep him.

stops.name: Camelot, the scabbard given and counterfeited
stops.campa: Merlin once told Arthur that the scabbard of Excalibur is worth ten of the sword, for while he wears it he shall never lose blood however sorely he is wounded, and bade him keep it always by him. So Arthur, for great trust, gave it instead to his sister. Morgan loves another knight better than her husband Uriens or her brother, and she would have Arthur slain; so she has a second scabbard made in its likeness by enchantment, hands the king the counterfeit, and keeps the true one for Accolon. No one at court will know the difference until a sword breaks that should not break.
stops.quote: Ye are more unwise, said Merlin, for the scabbard is worth ten of the swords, for whiles ye have the scabbard upon you, ye shall never lose no blood, be ye never so sore wounded; therefore keep well the scabbard always with you.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I, Chapter XXV (Caxton, 1485)

stops.name: The ship apparelled with silk, Accolon armed
stops.campa: Hunting a great hart, Arthur, King Uriens and Accolon of Gaul outride their fellowship by ten miles and kill their horses under them. On the water lies a little ship all apparelled with silk down to the waterline, empty of any earthly creature, and the three go aboard together. At dark a hundred torches spring alight, twelve fair damsels serve them the best supper of the king's life, and they are laid in three rich chambers and sleep marvellously sore. Uriens wakes in Camelot in his wife's arms; Arthur wakes in a dark prison; Accolon wakes by a deep well-side, half a foot from death, and a dwarf comes with Excalibur and Morgan's message.
stops.quote: Jesus save my lord King Arthur, and King Uriens, for these damosels in this ship have betrayed us, they were devils and no women.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book IV, Chapter VIII (Caxton, 1485)

stops.name: The duel of Arthur and Accolon
stops.campa: Arthur and Accolon meet as strangers, each fighting another man's quarrel, and only one of them carries the true sword. The false Excalibur shatters at the first hard blow, and Arthur, disarmed and bleeding under a rain of strokes he cannot answer, is a breath from death when the Damosel of the Lake, who owes Morgan no loyalty at all, makes the true sword fall out of Accolon's hand to the earth. Arthur leaps to it and knows it at once. Then he spies the scabbard hanging at Accolon's side, snatches it from him, and throws it from him as far as he can throw. Accolon does not survive what follows.

stops.name: Dozmary Pool, the scabbard cast away
stops.campa: Word of Accolon's death reaches Morgan before Arthur does, and she comes to where the king lies sleeping, takes the scabbard from beside him and rides out with forty horses. Arthur gives chase. When she sees she cannot escape she rides to a lake and throws the scabbard into the deepest of the water, and it sinks, for it is heavy of gold and precious stones. Then she rides into a valley full of great stones and shapes herself, horse and man, into one great marble stone. Arthur comes up, looks at the stones, says here may ye see the vengeance of God, and rides away sorry. When he is gone she turns them all back.
stops.quote: Whatsoever come of me, my brother shall not have this scabbard.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book IV, Chapter XIV (Caxton, 1485)

stops.name: Slaughterbridge, the Battle of Camlann
stops.campa: On the field by the River Camel the last battle is fought, Arthur against his own son Mordred, and by nightfall the flower of the Round Table lies dead on both sides and Mordred with them, and Arthur himself carries a wound that will not close, taken, the Annales Cambriae will one day simply record, in the year five hundred and thirty-seven. Of Morgan there is no word on this field; she is not a fighter, and the chroniclers, who have made her the architect of half the ruin that led here, do not bring her to see the wreck her hatred helped to build.

stops.name: Dozmary Pool, the return of Excalibur
stops.campa: Dying, Arthur commands Sir Bedivere three times to carry Excalibur to the water's edge and throw it in, and twice Bedivere, unable to lose so fair a sword to a pool, hides it instead and lies about it; the third time he obeys, and an arm clothed in white samite rises from the surface, catches the sword by the hilt, brandishes it three times, and draws it under. It is the same water, the country says, where Morgan once let the scabbard sink beyond finding; brother's sword and sister's sheath, given by the same hand years apart, come to rest at last in the one lake.

stops.name: The lakeshore, the barge and the three queens
stops.campa: They carry the king down to the water's edge, and there, close against the bank, a small barge waits with many fair ladies aboard it wearing black hoods, and among them three queens who cry out and weep the moment they see him laid low. One is his own sister, Morgan, come now not to steal but to receive. Arthur is set into the barge and lays his head in a queen's lap, and to the weeping Bedivere left standing on the shore he says only that he will go into the vale of Avilion to heal him of his grievous wound, and if Bedivere hear never more of him, to pray for his soul.
stops.quote: Comfort thyself, said the king, and do as well as thou mayst, for in me is no trust for to trust in; for I will into the vale of Avilion to heal me of my grievous wound: and if thou hear never more of me, pray for my soul.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter V (Caxton, 1485)

stops.name: Glastonbury Tor, the return to Avalon
stops.campa: The barge crosses out of the world of the chronicles and into the world of the Vita Merlini, arriving at the isle this journey has already stood on once: the green tor above the Summer Country, Ynys Witrin, the Island of Apples, where nine sisters keep an orchard that needs no farmer and Morgen keeps her chamber ready with its golden bed. Whether the king dies here or only sleeps, whether he wakes again or waits for Britain's greatest need, the canon will not choose; it leaves him, and leaves her beside him, in the one place built to hold a wound that healing cannot close and death will not claim.

stops.name: The Strait of Messina, the Fata Morgana
stops.campa: On calm mornings across the Strait of Messina, when the air lies in exact cold and warm layers over the water, the coast of Calabria seems to lift into the sky and unfold into castles, colonnades, whole cities hanging upside down and right side up at once, and the sailors who have watched it for a thousand years call it by her name alone: Fata Morgana, conjuring towers out of nothing to lure ships onto the rocks, or simply to be seen, as the tale tells it, by a Norman king who drowned believing the far shore was one stroke away. She has stopped being a woman in a story and become a weather.
